newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's opposition parties to fight press law.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's opposition parties to fight press law.

text.p: Jordan's parliamentary opposition parties said on Sunday they would try to press the government to withdraw a law introduced last week which tightened restrictions on the press.

Salem Nahas, coordinator of Jordan's Islamist, leftist, and Arab nationalist opposition parties, said the provisional law was unconstitutional because it was issued during parliament's pre-election recess.
"The Jordanian opposition parties pledge to continue to work to topple this law," Nahas told a news conference.
The amended press law, which set sweeping restrictions on reporting and stiffened fines for offenders, was the third issued in the space of one week without recourse to parliament.
It followed laws on investment reform and on the coming elections, scheduled for November.
Opposition parliamentarians and prominent union leaders have said the government had flouted Jordan's constitution and demanded that parliament be reconvened to discuss the laws.

Union bosses of Jordan's lawyers, engineers, dentists, and writers resigned in protest on Saturday, Jordanian newspapers said. Others have threatened to resign next month if the government does not revoke the press restrictions.
"This law is an attack on the legislative institutions," Islamist parliamentarian Mohammed Owaida said. "We will fight for it to be toppled."

Opposition parties, led by the Islamic Action Front, hold around 20 seats in parliament's 80-seat lower assembly. Islamists are also prominent in Jordan's professional unions, which have tens of thousands of members.

But Owaida said an opposition petition calling for a special parliamentary session had received only "modest" support so far and was well short of the 41 MPs' signatures needed for parliament to be recalled.
